record.file_problem: The full post is present. Some referenced plots are not included in the text, so their numerical values are not available.
record.tranche_reason: The post reports SAE feature-extraction results on Gemma 2B activations, extending indirect evidence about feature representations to an LLM setting; it does not reproduce the toy-model superposition method.
record.gate_note: The post also compares loss recovery, but that metric evaluates reconstruction performance rather than the claimed feature geometry. Its reported loss-recovery result is included under fits_no_version. Values used to define rarity and feature-quality scores are not reported numerically.
record.test_reason: The post uses SAEs as a tool and compares three ways of training domain-specific SAEs on Gemma 2B layer 12. Its measures are loss recovered, OWT feature rarity, max cosine similarity to GSAE features, and blind subject-specificity scores. All of these rank its own methods against each other. None asks whether features are superposed, spread across neurons, one-dimensional, or canonical units of the model. The rows are method comparisons, not tests of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. GSAE-finetune and Direct SAE recover loss best. SSAE finds rarer, newer and higher-rated features. The best choice depends on user needs. The results are tentative: one model, few datasets.
record.recipe_differences: Compares domain-specific SAE training strategies on an LLM's residual-stream activations; it does not use the toy-network superposition recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Results differ by SAE method and by measure: SSAE is described as better for rarity and subjective feature quality, while GSAE-finetune and Direct SAE tend to do better on loss recovery.

fits_no_version.finding: An SSAE trained on GSAE residuals on domain text finds features rarer on OWT and less similar to GSAE features. This implies the general 16x SAE missed domain-specific features. No numbers are given in the text.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: General-purpose SAEs of moderate width leave domain-specific features unrecovered, which targeted residual SAEs can find (feature coverage).

fits_no_version.finding: Finetuning a GSAE on domain data barely changes encoder rows or decoder columns, and the dashboards keep the same interpretations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features are largely preserved under domain finetuning from the same initialisation.

fits_no_version.finding: GSAE-finetune and Direct SAE marginally beat SSAE on fraction of loss recovered vs L0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reconstruction-loss recovery on domain data favours finetuned or direct SAEs over residual SSAEs.

record.problems: The author reports only one model and a small number of datasets. The text does not supply numerical values for the plotted rarity, novelty, or loss-recovery results, nor average human scores or uncertainty estimates. The feature-quality judgments are subjective, and the appendix's 'nice' labels are explicitly personal taste.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the individual subject Pareto curves or frequency histograms: the text summarizes their results across subjects without giving per-subject values. The post also mentions feature examples without reporting a separate measured outcome.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweep or geometry.
No neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity allocation.
Does not measure feature spread across neurons or whether sparse features exist. SAEs are assumed as a tool.
No completeness, seed-stability or canonicality test across independent dictionaries.

missing.what: SSAE feature-novelty histograms (max cosine similarity of SSAE and Direct SAE features to GSAE features). The text asserts SSAE features are 'newer', but no row records this and no values are given in the text.

record.verdict_notes: This is a methods post on SAE training for feature coverage, so it is T4. The reader's V4 and V5 'supports' labels are removed: method comparisons do not bear on whether superposition or canonical dictionary features hold. The footnote about feature count being bounded by parameter count is cited discussion, not a result.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-over-capacity sweep, overlap geometry, or sparsity-dependent transition is tested.
No neuron polysemanticity or allocation of dedicated versus shared dimensions by feature importance is measured.
No alternative causes of polysemantic neurons are tested.

Tests SAE-extracted domain features on one model and textbook datasets, but not how features spread across neurons, nor whether the extracted features are a complete inventory of the model's features.
Compares GSAE features with GSAE-finetune features in one setting, but does not test completeness or canonicality across seeds, models, or independently trained dictionaries.
Does not test whether model features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional subspaces.

rows.subject: Gemma 2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured OpenWebText activation frequencies of SAE features trained on domain-specific textbook data.

conditions.value: textbook datasets; includes economics and other subjects

rows.baseline: Typical GSAE-finetune and Direct SAE features
rows.value: The typical SSAE feature is described as much rarer on unstructured web text than typical GSAE-finetune or Direct SAE features.
rows.note: The post describes histograms but supplies no numerical frequencies in the text. It notes that the spike at 1e-8 represents dead features rounded up from zero.
rows.check: Compares OWT activation frequency across SAE training methods (SSAE vs GSAE-finetune/Direct SAE). This is a method comparison, not evidence that the LLM contains sparse recoverable features (V4).

rows.subject: Gemma 2B
rows.operation_detail: Human raters scored explanations of SAE features for subject-specificity.

conditions.value: 100 random features each from Direct SAE and SSAE

rows.measure: Average human subject-specificity score of feature explanations
rows.value: SSAE features tend to score higher than Direct SAE features; no average scores are stated.
rows.note: The explanations were based on top-activating examples from OpenWebText and math data. The post describes the scores as subjective and imperfect.
rows.check: Blind subject-specificity ratings compare SSAE with Direct SAE on college math. This is method performance, not a measure of superposition or feature spread. No average scores are given in the text.

rows.subject: Gemma 2B
rows.operation_detail: Compared human subject-specificity scores for SAE feature explanations.
rows.value: The post says the biology results were similar to the college-math results, where SSAE features tended to score higher; no scores are stated.
rows.note: The biology comparison is summarized without sample counts or numerical scores.
rows.check: Same method comparison on biology. The post says the results were 'similar', and no scores are given. The 'partial' state has no basis.

rows.subject: Gemma 2B
rows.operation_detail: Counted features marked especially nice during blind human feature labelling.

conditions.value: 200 SSAE features and Direct SAE features

rows.measure: Count of features marked especially nice
rows.note: The author says this selection was mostly for fun and purely based on personal taste; the denominator for the Direct SAE count is not stated.
rows.check: Count of 'nice' features (22/200 SSAE vs 7 Direct SAE) is explicitly personal taste and 'mostly for fun'. It should not be a main row; at most it is anecdotal. The Direct SAE denominator is probably also 200 (100 math + 100 biology), but this is not stated.

rows.subject: Gemma 2B
rows.operation_detail: Compared each GSAE-finetune decoder column's maximum cosine similarity with GSAE decoder columns.
rows.measure: Maximum decoder-column cosine similarity to a GSAE feature
rows.value: The post describes GSAE-finetune features as very similar to GSAE features; no numerical similarities are stated.
rows.note: The text says the plots for other subjects looked identical, but the reported example is high-school physics.
rows.check: Similarity of GSAE-finetune decoders to the GSAE shows that finetuning barely moves features. It does not test V5's completeness or canonicality across independently trained dictionaries. Same-initialisation finetuning is not an independent stability test.

rows.subject: Gemma 2B
rows.operation_detail: Compared each GSAE-finetune encoder row's maximum cosine similarity with GSAE encoder rows.
rows.measure: Maximum encoder-row cosine similarity to a GSAE feature
rows.value: The post describes GSAE-finetune features as very similar to GSAE features, particularly for encoder comparisons; no numerical similarities are stated.
rows.note: The author says the encoder weights hardly change during finetuning and that feature dashboards have the same interpretations.
rows.check: Same as r5 for encoder rows. This is a finetuning-dynamics observation, not V5 stability or canonicality.

rows.subject: Gemma 2B

rows.value: GSAE-finetune and Direct SAE tend to marginally outperform SSAE.
rows.note: The text summarizes Pareto curves without numerical values. This measures reconstruction performance, not superposition geometry or feature completeness.
